                                            Abstract. Witness encryption encrypts a message to an NP statement so that whoever holds a witness
                                            can decrypt. Over a decade after its introduction, known constructions for general NP statements are far
                                            from practical or rest on heuristic or broken assumptions. We propose Praxis, a practical scheme for NP,
                                            and prove it extractable in the bilinear generic group and random oracle models under Module-SIS. Our
                                            instantiation encrypts to a Groth16 verifier on BN254, set up honestly, which serves every NP relation at
                                                                                                                                                                             34.2
                                            thesamecost:at100-bitsecurity,itsciphertextis7.88GiB,encryptiontakes2                                                                  base-field multiplications,
                                                                                                             33.0
                                            and decryption with a Groth16 proof 2                                  on average. We give Lean 4 proofs of correctness and extraction
                                            at this instantiation’s parameters.
                                            Praxis starts from the rank-gap template of the recent feasibility result [Hair and Sahai, arXiv 2026].
                                            Wheretheyraise the gap to keep decryption polynomial, we fix it, so decryption ends with a search that is
                                                                                                        𝜆/4    1/4
                                            exponential but concretely fast: 𝑂(2                            𝑁      ) expected operations for a statement in 𝑁 Boolean unknowns
                                            at 𝜆-bit security. A quadratic arithmetic program makes our hidden matrix low rank, so where their
                                            ciphertext encodes a basis of a matrix space, ours holds factors of width two, which a pairing multiplies.
                                            Weights and identities from an extension field tie copies of this matrix, so an adversary telling encryptions
                                            apart yields a witness or a Module-SIS solution. For the same Groth16 statement and 100-bit security
                                            level, Praxis reduces the ciphertext size and the cost of encryption of either of their constructions by over
                                            ten orders of magnitude, and that of decryption by over six.

                          1 Introduction
                          Witness encryption [GGSW13] encrypts a message to a statement instead of a key: anyone holding a witness
                          of the statement can decrypt, and if the statement is false the message stays hidden. The statement can be
                          any NP statement, for instance that a program accepts some input, and any input it accepts is a witness.
                          Aciphertext carries its own release condition, with no key to distribute and no party trusted to release the
                          message. Its applications include public-key, identity-based, and attribute-based encryption [GGSW13], time-
                          lock encryption that opens once a blockchain reaches a given length [LJKW18], one-time programs [GG17],
                          and, on Bitcoin, bridges without a custodian [Hio22], proof verification [GKSST26], and covenants [Abd+26].
                          Garg, Gentry, Sahai, and Waters introduced witness encryption in 2013, with a puzzle as the statement, so
                          that whoever solves it can read the message even after the encryptor is gone. Later that year, Goldwasser et
                          al. [GKPVZ13] strengthened it to extractable witness encryption, in which an adversary that tells encryptions
                          of two messages apart yields a witness.
                               Since then, every construction has had at most two of three properties: generality, for all of NP; proved
                          security in well-studied models and under well-studied assumptions; and practical costs. The general con-
                          structions with such proofs are feasibility results, far from practical. Witness encryption follows from indis-
                          tinguishability obfuscation [GGHRSW13], which exists under well-founded assumptions [JLS21], and, in the
                          generic group model (GGM), from a hypothesis on linear codes [BIOW20] and, by Hair and Sahai, from a
                          rank gap that they prove [HS26]. In their construction, a witness passes a set of linear tests with a matrix
                          of rank one, while on a false statement every nonzero matrix that passes has rank at least 𝑑, a gap of one
                          versus 𝑑. The practical schemes with proofs handle restricted relations, such as signatures or openings of
                          commitments [DHMW23; FHS24]. The other constructions for NP lack the second property, as they rest
                          on heuristic arguments [BĲMSZ20] or on purpose-built assumptions [GLW14; Tsa22], many of them since
                          attacked [CHLRS15; DJMMV25], or have been broken [CWLHTM25] (Section 1.3).
                               Praxis has all three properties, and is the first witness encryption scheme that does. It encrypts to any NP
                          statement, and we prove it extractable in the bilinear generic group and random oracle (RO) models under
                          Module-SIS (MSIS). It is also practical. At the 100-bit security level, with one fixed Groth16 [Gro16] key
                          whose verifier serves every NP relation, its ciphertext is 7.88GiB, and encryption takes seconds on a laptop,
                          as does decryption given a Groth16 proof. A witness leaves the decryptor one secret integer to find, by a
                          search exponential in the security parameter yet concretely short; anyone without a witness must guess four
                          such integers at once, an exponentially longer search, unless they solve MSIS. Praxis starts from Hair and
                          Sahai’s construction. For the same statement and security level, their basic construction [HS26, Theorem 5.1],
                                                                                                                                                11
                          a variant of a construction proved extractable [Cam26], needs over 1.1 × 10                                               GiB to encrypt a 100-bit key
                          (Table 1).

                            To encrypt, one fixes the instance, a program with its public inputs and outputs, as constants of this system;
                            a proof for that instance then decrypts, and knowledge soundness turns an extracted proof into a witness
                            of the relation. That step assumes an honest Groth16 setup, whose secret randomness would let whoever
                            kept it decrypt every ciphertext made for that key (Section 6.1). With this verifier, Praxis builds on the
                            modern infrastructure of zero-knowledge proofs: statements written as R1CS [BCGTV13], CCS [STW23],
                            Plonkish [GWC19], or AIR [BBHR18] are proved by arguments whose proofs the universal argument verifies,
                            and zero-knowledge virtual machines whose proofs end in Groth16 [Suc26; RIS24] prove the execution of
                            programs written in ordinary languages. So one can even encrypt to a program written in Rust: whoever
                            knows an input that the program accepts can decrypt.
                            Main result (informal). We represent a Groth16 verifier on BN254 as a BQS. For this system, at security
                            level 𝜆 = 100, Praxis has these properties.

                                Witness key encapsulation. Decryption recovers a group element from which an RO derives a key of
                                 any length, so Praxis is a witness key encapsulation mechanism (WKEM) [CV21]. A symmetric cipher under
                                 that key then encrypts messages of any length.

                                 1.2        From the Rank Template to Praxis
                                 Both of Hair and Sahai’s constructions [HS26] rest on what we call the rank template: the conditions on a
                                witness are linear tests on its moment matrix, the matrix of the products of pairs of its entries, and a witness
                                 passes them with a matrix of rank one. On a false statement every nonzero matrix that passes, a cheat, has
                                                                                                                                                 ⊤
                                 higher rank. The template’s table is the hidden matrix 𝑦𝑟 , with an entry for each pair of unknowns, for a
                                 hidden uniform vector 𝑦 and a vector 𝑟 of small secret integers, and decryption ends with a bounded search
                                                                𝑟(𝑤) = ∑                 𝑟   for the witness                  . The search is why the unknowns are Boolean: confining
                                 for one integer,                                     𝑤                                      𝑤
                                                                                         𝑖  𝑖
                                                                                    𝑖
                                 each 𝑤 to 0 and 1, with one quadratic test, is the cheapest way to keep this integer in a short known range.
                                              𝑖
                                 For a cheat of rank 𝑑, 𝑑 combinations of the secret integers must be guessed together, which succeeds with
                                                                          −𝑑
                                 probability at most 𝑔                         when each secret integer has a range of 𝑔 values (Lemma 4.5), and for some cheats
                                                                                                                                        4

                              a generic search finds them in about 𝑔                                     group operations. So the least rank 𝑑 of a cheat sets the range,

                                    Hair and Sahai keep the range 𝑔 polynomial in the size of their ciphertexts, so that decryption takes time
                              polynomial in that size, and make the rank of every cheat high. With one table, a cheat can have rank two,
                              so they stack many copies of the table, each weighted by a product of linear forms in the witness, until every
                              cheat has rank above a threshold 𝑅. A ciphertext carries one bit, and in both of their constructions three
                              features set its size; we give the counts for their basic construction [HS26, Theorem 5.1], the construction
                              of Table 1. First, with a polynomial range, 𝑅 must grow with the security level, at more copies for each list
                              of forms (Appendix C). Second, the ciphertext holds one element for each matrix in a basis of the passing
                                                                               2
                              matrices, on the order of 𝑁                        for one table and a system of linear size [HS26, Sections 3.1 and 4]. Third, to
                              rule out a matrix of rank at most 𝑅 as a cheat, their proof needs a list of 𝑅 forms that are not all zero at any
                              nonzero vector of its row space. The forms are fixed before a cheat is known, so the copies come in 2𝑁𝑅+1
                                                                                                                  3
                              lists, and for fixed 𝑅 the ciphertext grows as 𝑁                                     [HS26, Sections 5.2 and 5.3] (Proposition C.1).
                                    Praxis replaces these three features in four steps, and Table 2 gives the costs after each.
                              1. One table: a fixed rank gap, a wide range, and a key in the corner (Section 2.2). Where Hair and Sahai
                                   raise the rank, we fix the rank gap and take a range 𝑔 exponential in 𝜆. Size and encryption then stay
                                   polynomial in 𝜆, at the price of a search exponential in 𝜆, by baby steps and giant steps [Sha71]. We
                                   publish their table entry by entry, the form that step 2 factors. Anyone can combine its entries, with any
                                   matrix as coefÏcients, and a test mask, a random combination of the tests, makes the result useless unless
                                   that matrix passes. We put a key in the table’s corner, where a witness’s moment matrix has the entry
                                   1, so a ciphertext carries a key and not one bit. The key itself is not published, so a second copy of the
                                   ciphertext, scaled by a hidden factor, comes with its scaled key, which the decryptor subtracts before the
                                                                                                                                                      𝜆                                                      𝜆/2    1/4
                                   search. With this one table, cheats of rank two remain, so 𝑔 ≈ 2                                                      and the search takes about 2                             𝑁
                                   operations, while the ciphertext is quadratic in 𝑁.
                              2. Two factors, from a quadratic arithmetic program (QAP) that takes sums of products (Sections 2.3 and 4.4).
                                   Thetest mask can have high rank, so the table takes one element for each entry. We replace the test mask
                                   andthekeybyonetermofrankone:thevalues,atahiddenpoint,ofthepolynomialsofaQAP[GGPR13]
                                   that encodes the tests. The table then has rank at most two, and we publish two factors of it, of width
                                   two, in the two source groups of a pairing. A pairing, which Hair and Sahai’s model lacks, multiplies
                                                                                                                                                           2
                                   them, so its two factors take 4(𝑁 + 1) elements in place of (𝑁 + 1) entries. The table is never formed.
                                   The encryptor computes only the factors, and a decryptor with a witness combines each factor with it
                                   before pairing, so the table’s share of encryption and decryption is linear in 𝑁 too. This puts no limit on
                                   the rank of a cheat, which is a matrix of coefÏcients for the table’s entries, not the table. The factored
                                   table is not symmetric, so a matrix that is not symmetric could pass with rank one; a new symmetry
                                   term masks every combination along such a matrix, without widening the factors. A hidden change of
                                   basis between the factors, as in dual pairing vector spaces [OT08; OT09] and canceling pairings [Fre10],
                                   cancels only in whole entries, so an adversary cannot weight an entry’s two products differently. A BQS
                                   constraint sums many products, as in customizable constraint systems (CCS) of degree two, while the
                                   QAPofGennaro et al. has one product in each constraint, as a rank-one constraint system (R1CS) does.
                                   Rewriting our constraints in that form would need an auxiliary unknown, a field element of 254 bits, for
                                   each product but one, so the unknowns, and the costs with them, can grow by a factor of order 𝜆, to
                                     29.1                                                           18.6
                                   2        Boolean unknowns in place of 2                                 for our statement. Our QAP takes sums of products directly: it
                                   places a constraint’s products on a coset of a multiplicative subgroup, over which their terms must sum
                                   to zero, and checks these sums by allowing its division a remainder with no exponent divisible by the
                                   coset’s size. A test that an unknown is Boolean takes one point, not a coset, keeping the number of points
                                   𝑂(𝑁) for systems of linear size. Our QAP builds on Aurora’s sum over a coset [BCRSVW19], read for
                                   all cosets at once [Moh25], and on a vanishing sum enforced through the reference string [LSZ22; ZSG24].
                                   One factored table takes 0.14GiB, but its search is about as long as step 1’s.
                              3. Tied copies: weights and ties under MSIS, with the weights from an extension field (Sections 2.4 and 5.1).
                                   To shorten the search, we raise the least rank of an easily guessed cheat from two to four. Like Hair and
                                   Sahai [HS26, Section 4], we weight copies of the table by polynomials in the witness, built from linear
                                   forms. One table lets a cheat mix the moment matrices of two assignments so that their violations of each
                                   constraint cancel, and under the weights they would have to cancel in every copy. Three things are ours.
                                   First, an adversary can combine each of our copies along a matrix of its own, even one cheat repeated

                                 copies’ tables differ only in a scalar, the product of a left and a right scalar. So the copies are the cells of a
                                 grid, those in one row or one column share a factor, and the factors take 528 elements for each unknown.
                                 The price, none in growth, is in the masks: a column’s mask serves every row, and one more hidden coin
                                 marks the mixed products that this leaves, so that published elements remove them but not the terms
                                 that enforce the ties. The grid returns a factor of order 𝜆 in size and in encryption, and of order 𝜆/log𝜆
                                 in decryption outside the search. In all, the copies cost Praxis a factor 𝜆 in size and in encryption over

                            1.3       Related Work
                            Feasibility results.                      Besides obfuscation [GGHRSW13], which exists under well-founded assump-
                            tions [JLS21; RVV24], witness encryption follows from subexponentially hard learning with errors (LWE),
                                                                  𝑚/2
                            with encryption time 2                       for witnesses of 𝑚 bits [BJKPW18]. The approach of building witness encryption
                            in a generic group from NP-hardness of approximation is due to Barta et al. [BIOW20]. In their scheme
                            a witness is a nonzero codeword of low Hamming weight, which passes a hidden linear test by missing the
                            ciphertext’s sparse noise; security needs a gap of 𝜔(log𝑛) for the minimum distance of linear codes, which
                            is not known to be NP-hard. Hair and Sahai, who name it their closest generic-group precursor, replace
                                                                                                                     6
                                         Hamming weight by matrix rank and sparse noise by small secret integers and a bounded search, prove the
                                         gap they need, and so need no further assumption in prime-order generic groups [HS26]; Jin builds on Barta
                                         et al. [Jin26] (Section 1.1).
                                         Restricted relations. Other schemes, most of them pairing-based, handle restricted relations or interfaces:
                                         algebraic languages [DS18], openings of KZG commitments [FHS24], signatures [DHMW23; ADMSW24],
                                         functional commitments [CFK24], linearly verifiable succinct arguments [GHKKP25], invalid proofs of
                                         pairing-based SNARKs [EL26], proof verification on Bitcoin [GKSST26], and the SAT instances that resist
                                         mixed-input attacks, with a variant for all instances in which the encryptor or a third party takes part in
                                         decryption [WWZ24]. Groth shows that, in his model, two-move linear interactive proofs with exact correct-
                                         ness cannot have a linear decision procedure for relations with hard decisional problems [Gro16, Theorem 3];
                                         our decryption, ending with a bounded search for one integer, is not such a procedure.
                                         Candidates on heuristic or purpose-built assumptions.                                                                                                                  The first constructions of witness en-
                                         cryption [GGSW13; GLW14] use multilinear maps, whose candidates met zeroizing and annihilation at-
                                         tacks [CHLRS15; HJ16; MSZ16]; one such scheme was implemented, for Sudoku puzzles [ULCG21]. Lattice
                                         candidates [CVW18; Klu20; Tsa22; VWW22] rest on purpose-built assumptions, some of them on evasive
                                         LWE, for which counterexamples are known [BÜW24; DJMMV25; AMYY25]. The scheme built from afÏne
                                         determinant programs [BĲMSZ20] rests on heuristic arguments, and so does its arithmetic variant [Sou+26],
                                         whose authors estimate a ciphertext of about 338TiB at 100-bit security. Attacks recover the message from
                                         the ciphertext for the original candidate [Jo26] and, for sparse circuits, in both [ERSS26]; the latter attack
                                         is by authors of the variant. The variant’s first author has since proposed a patch meant to resist it [Sou26],
                                         which also rests on heuristic arguments and claims no ciphertext size.
                                         Broken proposals. Pairing-based proposals for general NP statements come with security proofs. Yet
                                         in the WKEM of Chang et al. [CWLHTM25], built from a QAP and the verification equation of Groth16,
                                         the key can be computed from the statement and the ciphertext without a witness [Van25]. The same
                                         write-up states that this also holds for the similar scheme of Wang and Zhang [WZ25]. A scheme from
                                         smooth projective hashing [WZ22] encrypts to a Groth16 proof that the decryptor has already computed,
                                         and decryption needs that proof’s randomness, so a ciphertext is addressed to the one prover that made it,
                                         not to every holder of a witness. Its hash function is also not smooth, since the projection key contains the
                                         hash key in the exponent.
                                         Relaxed notions. OfÒine witness encryption [AFP16] makes encryption fast but not its obfuscation-based
                                         setup or decryption, and in Cassiopeia [SZ23] a committee releases the message when shown a witness.
                                         2 Technical Overview
                                         Astatement is a system of quadratic equations over the field 𝔽 of prime order 𝑞 in Boolean unknowns, and
                                         Praxis works in a bilinear group of order 𝑞. We first turn the system into linear tests on a matrix, which a
                                         witness passes with a matrix of rank one (Section 2.1). We restate the rank template of Hair and Sahai [HS26]
                                         with a test mask, a random combination of the tests, and give it a fixed rank gap, a wide range, and a key in
                                         the table’s corner (Section 2.2). We then replace the test mask with a quadratic arithmetic program (QAP),
                                         so that the table is virtual, defined by two factors of width two, which a pairing multiplies, and let the QAP
                                         take sums of products (Section 2.3). We weight and tie many copies of the table so that, under Module-SIS
                                        (MSIS), no adversary forms an easily guessed cheat of rank below four (Section 2.4), and let the copies share
                                         their factors (Section 2.5). Sections 2.2 to 2.5 follow the four steps of Table 2, and Table 1 compares Praxis
                                         with Hair and Sahai’s construction. For ease of exposition, three constructions that Table 2 prices are given
                                         in full only in later sections: the QAP for constraints that sum products (Section 4.4), the weights from an
                                         extension field (Section 5.1), and the masks that enforce the ties on shared factors (Section 5.1).
                                         Notation. Vectors with an entry for each index 0,…,𝑁 are lowercase, as in 𝑤 = (𝑤 ,…,𝑤 ), and matrices

                                                2.2             The Rank Template
                                               This subsection recalls how Hair and Sahai turn the tests into witness encryption, and restates their scheme
                                                in the form that Praxis builds on: a table 𝑇 under a test mask 𝑀, with a key 𝜅 in its corner and a bounded
                                                search in decryption. We then show that the least rank 𝑑 of a cheat sets the range 𝑔 of the secret integers
                                                𝑟 , and with it the cost of decryption, and that one table has a ciphertext quadratic in 𝑁; the next two

                                                   The least rank of a cheat sets the range. The argument of Hair and Sahai [HS26, Lemma 3.4 and
                                                   Theorem 3.5] in the generic group model (GGM), adapted to our table, says that on a system without
                                                   witnesses, apart from identities, coincidences in 𝔽, and encodings guessed at random, a comparison of two
                                                    combinations of the published elements succeeds only if it amounts to a correct guess of 𝑊𝑟 for a nonzero
                                                    passing matrix 𝑊, that is, for a cheat. So an adversary gains only by choosing a cheat and guessing its
                                                    numbers. One guess is right with probability at most gp(𝑊), and 𝑄 group operations, once 𝑄 is at least the
                                                    number of published elements, give a number of comparisons quadratic in 𝑄. If every cheat has gp(𝑊) ≤ 𝜃,

                                  3.5         Witness Encryption
                                  Let ℛ be an NP relation: a set of pairs (𝑆,𝑤) of an instance 𝑆 and a witness 𝑤, decidable in time poly(|𝑆|),
                                  with |𝑤| ≤ poly(|𝑆|), where |𝑆| is the length of an encoding of 𝑆. An indexed relation, of triples (𝑖,𝑥,𝑤)
                                  with an index 𝑖 such as a circuit or a program and a public input 𝑥 that may include claimed outputs, is
                                  used through its pairs ((𝑖,𝑥),𝑤), so that its instances are 𝑆 = (𝑖,𝑥). For Praxis, ℛ pairs Boolean quadratic
                                  systems (BQS) of a fixed shape (Section 4) with their witnesses, the Boolean assignments that satisfy every
                                  constraint (Definition 4.1). An index and a public input enter such a system only as its constants.
                                  Definition 3.4 (Witness encryption). A witness encryption scheme for an NP relation ℛ and messages

                                                4.4             The QAP of a System
                                               The quadratic arithmetic program (QAP) of Gennaro et al. [GGPR13] is an R1CS in polynomial form: each
                                                constraint, with its one product, sits at its own point, and exact division by the points’ vanishing polynomial
                                                checks them all. Ours places at each point a pair (𝑎,𝑏) of vectors, which stands for the product 𝑎(𝑤)𝑏(𝑤); the
                                                                                                                                      ⊤
                                                pair’s term on a matrix 𝑊 is 𝑎 𝑊 𝑏, and each test sets a sum of terms to zero. The pairs of each constraint’s
                                                test sit on its own coset of one subgroup, and an allowed remainder replaces exact division, so a constraint
                                                can sum many products without the auxiliary unknowns of an R1CS rewrite, which can multiply the number
                                                of unknowns, and so the costs, by Θ(𝜆) (Section 2.1). Section 2.3 worked out only the case of an R1CS, with
                                                the subgroup {1,−1}: a pair of points for each constraint and for each Booleanity test. The pieces are known:
                                                the coset sum behind Aurora’s univariate sumcheck [BCRSVW19], read for all cosets at once [Moh25], and
                                                a vanishing sum enforced through the reference string [LSZ22; ZSG24]; our QAP combines them. Fix a coset
                                               size 𝜈 that divides 𝑞 − 1 and exceeds 𝐹                                                                                 ; we take the least power of two above 𝐹                                                                                      , so that 𝜈 ≤ 2𝐹                                       .
                                                                                                                                                                 max                                                                                                                            max                                                     max
                                               Write 𝐷 for the number 𝑁 +2+𝜈𝑛 of evaluation points.

                                 Definition 5.3 (Centered sampler). For an integer 𝑔 ≥ 1 with 𝑔 +1 < 𝑞, the centered sampler 𝒟 draws

                             6 Instantiation
                             6.1       Witness Encryption for R1CS via Groth16
                             Praxis’s ciphertext and costs grow with the system, and so with the relation. As instantiated here, following
                             Goldwasser et al. [GKPVZ13] and Liu et al. [LJKW18], Praxis encrypts to the verifier of a succinct argument
                             of knowledge, with its verification key and public inputs fixed. A decryptor computes a proof from its witness;
                             the proof’s bits and those of the verifier’s intermediate values solve its system.
                                   Any argument of knowledge with a fully succinct verifier, whose size does not depend on the program,
                             would serve. We use Groth16 [Gro16] on BN254, its verifier over 𝔽 . Its setup is per circuit, so we fix one key,
                                                                                                                                                𝑞
                             for a universal argument of knowledge, which proves that a program accepts an input and witness within a
                             time bound, the program and input public. All relations share this setup, one system up to constants, and so
                             the ciphertext size and cost bounds given a proof. A universal circuit gives one key for fixed program, input,
                             and time bounds [BCTV14], so universality needs no assumption beyond Groth16’s knowledge soundness.
                             In practice, as in SP1 [Suc26], the circuit instead verifies a faster-proving argument designed in the RO
                             model, and using it would add an assumption, the knowledge soundness of this recursion, for which that
                             model offers no proof [BCG25]. Such arguments take statements as CCS [STW23], Plonkish [GWC19], or an
                             algebraic intermediate representation (AIR) [BBHR18], and SP1 proves the execution of programs written
                             in languages such as Rust. We assume Groth16’s knowledge soundness, with an honest setup (Table 5), for
                             the adversary followed by our extractor, as long as the two together cost less than a discrete logarithm on
                             BN254 (Section 6.2), which would reveal the setup’s trapdoor, with which one can make accepting proofs
                                                                                                            37
                             for every public input. At the extractor’s 2                                         operations a call, by Lean’s count (Theorem 5.9(c)), this
                                                                                              65                           100
                             covers adversaries that make up to 2                                  calls in time 2              , precomputation included. Precomputation counts
                             because, with one fixed key, advice could otherwise hold the setup’s trapdoor or an accepting proof for a
                             false statement, and every public input has accepting proofs. Whoever ran the setup and kept its trapdoor
                             can also make such proofs, and so decrypt every ciphertext made for this key. Praxis’s Setup is deterministic,
                             with no secret (Section 5.1). For concreteness, our counts use SP1’s 6.1.0 key as a stand-in for any Groth16
                             key on BN254: 𝑁 = 391,693 Boolean unknowns and 1,692 constraints in our encoding; other keys give nearly
                             the same. For this key, the encoding is built so that every solution decodes to a proof the verifier accepts,
                             and a computer check confirms the bounds that make its arithmetic in BN254’s base field exact. We also
                             tested the encoder on proofs under many other keys against independent implementations of the verifier.
                             6.2       Parameters and Concrete Security

                   Running time. As usual in the generic model, Lean counts an adversary’s oracle calls but not its com-

                   The reductions. Like those of Appendix B.5, Lean’s reductions program 𝐻                        at one fresh seed; they
                                                                                                              seed

                                 0        1
                   Axioms. Lean’s kernel checks the proofs, built on Mathlib [Mat20] and VCVio [TDWHH26], with only
                   the three standard axioms that make Lean’s type theory classical: propositional extensionality, quotient
                   soundness, and choice.
                   Acknowledgments. This paper is the result of a research process carried out with AI, mostly in the weeks since Hair
                   and Sahai’s paper [HS26] appeared; it began by interrogating their construction and then trying to build on it. We used
                   Claude and GPT to assist with the research and to draft text and proofs. The research ideas are ours, as are some of the
                   directions and techniques and the main ideas for the improvements; for the most part, the models worked out the details
                   of how to carry them out. For example, our earlier work on zero-knowledge proofs led us to suggest the techniques based
                   on QAPs, and we suggested extracting a solution of the system as a way to rule out low ranks; in both cases, the models
                   worked out the concrete approach. We also found a number of simplifications of the scheme, and we distilled the results
                   into the set of techniques and the methodology the paper presents. The models also wrote the Lean proofs and checked
                   the proofs and computations. We take full responsibility for the paper and its contents.

                        Records. The reductions and the extractor follow the answered calls and keep for a label of each group a
                        computable record of an expression: a reduction its value at a point and its formula in the calls, the extractor
                        its sketch data. They start from the received labels, give an operand without a record that of 0, which it
                        keeps, compute the record of a result from those of its operands, and keep it if its label has none. Until the
                        monitor sets a mark, a label with a record has an entry X, and the record is that of an expression formally
                                       ∘
                        equal to X ; an entry whose label has no record is a guess variable that no answered call had as an operand,
                                                                                         ∘
                        so it occurs in no result. By induction: X ↦ X commutes with linear combinations and pairings, and a result
                        that sets no mark meets no entry or one formally equal to it. So at a first mark diff(D), set by a result F at a
                        label with the entry X, the label has a record, at the latest from this call if it is one of its operands, as F−X
                        has no guess variable, and the result’s record minus the label’s is that of D, up to formal equality. Formally
                        equal expressions of 𝔾            have equal stacks, by Lemma B.4(a) for their difference at every 𝑟, so equal sketches.

                        Each reduction ℬ of Theorem 5.9 tries up to two expressions from a private monitor and, if one is a good

                                         B.7 Proof of the Inverse Theorem
                                         This subsection proves Lemma B.7; symbols other than the lemma’s are local to it. Reading the nonzero
                                         coordinates of 𝑣 one at a time, we keep a saturated integer lattice of rank at most three whose reduction
                                         modulo 𝑞 contains the prefix read, with a fiber at most 3𝜀                                                                                           less dense than the densest set on which that
                                                                                                                                                                                          tr
                                         prefix is constant modulo 𝑞. To add a coordinate, we trim that set for the longer prefix to an ellipsoid: a
                                         count of lattice points shows that its congruence cannot wrap around modulo 𝑞, so small minors make it
                                         hold over the integers, which gives the next lattice; a regularization bounds the product of fiber density and
                                         height that the count needs. Each step starts from the densest set of its own prefix and inherits only a lattice,
                                         so losses do not accumulate. Minkowski’s theorem in the last lattice gives the short multiple.
                                                                                                                                                                                                               𝐼
                                         Boxes and prefixes. For a finite set 𝐼, the box on 𝐼 is [2,𝑔 + 1] , and 𝑟 is uniform on it, as 𝑟 ,…,𝑟
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   𝐼                                                       1               𝑁

                                            C Comparison with Hair and Sahai
                                            Wecompare with Hair and Sahai’s constructions set up beyond what their theorems allow, and extend their
                                            proof to show that these settings still meet the security level. Each choice is in their favor, and the paragraph
                                            that makes it gives its reason:
                                            – the least parameters that their bound certifies for 𝜆-bit security, where their theorems fix larger ones: the
                                                   threshold 𝑅 of their Theorem 5.1, and the degree and weight degree of their Theorem 6.1, which their
                                                   proof leaves free;
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             𝑚
                                            – a group whose order has Θ(𝜆) bits, where their theorems take 𝑝 ≥ 2 , as their proof needs only three
                                                   conditions on the order;
                                            – our decryption search in place of their list of multiples;
                                            – our fixed-base scalar multiplication, 11 afÏne additions at our parameters, where their paper takes 𝑂(log𝑝)
                                                   group operations [HS26, Section 3.1];
                                            – counts that are lower bounds: the published elements, the scalar multiplications that make them, and
                                                   the group operations of decryption, but not 𝑍 or their arithmetic in 𝔽 , and with the dimension 𝑘 of 𝑆
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               𝑝
                                                   bounded from below.
                                            Their section, equation, and statement numbers are those of the third version of their paper [HS26], and
                                            logarithms have base two.

                      Additions are 1.0 to 1.8 times the multiplications in each total of either scheme. Neither scheme’s counts
                  include point decompression, as both sizes are of compressed elements; counting it for us alone keeps decryp-
                  tion over five orders of magnitude apart. Hashing and memory trafÏc, left out of both counts, are small for
                  us (Section 6.3) and for them would only add to costs we bound from below.
                  Onebit and a key. Their scheme as stated carries one bit per ciphertext: the decryptor’s two elements, 𝐻
                  and 𝑍, depend on the witness, so neither can serve as a key. Our key in the corner (Section 2.2) would likely
                                                                                                            2
                  remove this limit. In each of their constructions, the copy of weight 1 has the entry 𝑤 = 1 for every witness,
                                                                                                            0
                  so the encryptor could add 𝜅 times that entry of each basis matrix; a witness’s combination would then
                  encode 𝜅 plus the search term, which a published check of [𝜅] or a second, key-free copy lets the decryptor
                  remove. An adversary’s element would encode 𝜅 only along a nonzero matrix, of rank at least 𝑑 on a false
                  statement, as in their Lemma 3.4, but neither their paper nor ours proves this variant. A key would then
                  cost one or two of their one-bit ciphertexts in place of 100, and their costs would still be over eight orders
                  of magnitude above ours in size and encryption and over four in decryption.
